per_ply.human_comment:
In 1884 the magazine "Vsemirnaia Illiustrazia", in which the chess
column was held by Chigorin himself, organized a correspondence chess
tournament. There were 12 participants, each playing two game with everyone
else. The tournament was easily won by Chigorin with 20 wins and 2 draws, 4
points ahead of the runner up. The games were then published, and the
following game started a lot of lively discussions in the press in many
countries.
per_ply.system_comment: The game opens as a King's Pawn Game (B00).
The game transposes into the King's Knight Opening (C40).
The game transposes into the Italian Game (C50).
The game transposes into the Evans Gambit Accepted, 5.c3 (C51).
The game transposes into the Italian Game: Evans Gambit, McDonnell Defense (C51).

The most accurate move targets the bishop on c5 and holds the balance (+0.00, Stockfish:16) after [pv:d4 Bb6 dxe5 dxe5 Qxd8+], at the cost of a pawn structure that could later feature doubled, isolated, and backward pawns. Bb5 was a comparable option that leads to equality after [pv:Bb5 Bd7 Bxc6 Bxc6 d4], pinning a piece and targeting the knight on c6, but d4 is the stronger way to keep immediate pressure on that bishop.

per_ply.human_comment:
This simple developing move
was Chigorin's favourite one and proved to be the right one.

Now, however, this Knight
jump near the fence is not so good and makes a lot of troubles to its
conductor.  Right was 9... Bg4 10. Bb5 Kf8 (!) 11. Be3 Nge7 and Black would
have kept his extra pawn and a solid position.

per_ply.system_comment: This is the last book move of the Italian Game: Evans Gambit, Göring Attack (C51); both sides are on their own from here.

Black's most accurate move holds the balance (+0.00, Stockfish:16) after [pv:Ne7 Bd3 O-O Nd5 Nac6], setting up a fight against the knight on d5 in the line, at the cost of a continuation that may leave a piece hanging and could expose the back rank—king pressure along such lines often forces awkward defense later. f6 is a comparable option that leads to equality via [pv:f6 Bf4 Nxc4 Qa4+ Kf7], leaving White's pieces passive immediately while the line may yield a bishop and pawn for a knight.

per_ply.human_comment: A risky decision. Against Steinitz our hero played the stronger move 12.Bf4.
per_ply.system_comment: The most accurate move holds the balance, as 12.Bxf6 is set to leave Black's king under pressure along the main line—king pressure often forces the defender to spend tempi on safety rather than active play. (+0.00, Stockfish:16) [pv:Bxf6 gxf6 Nxf6+ Kf8 Ng5] Nh4 was a comparable option that leads to a slight advantage for Black [pv:Nh4 Nxd5 Qh5+ Kd7 Bxd5].

Black's 13...Kf8 holds the balance (+0.00, Stockfish:16) after [pv:Kf8 Qc1 Ng8 Nh5 Nxc4], consolidating the bishop-for-pawn edge already on the board—a material gain that typically gives the side up the exchange genuine winning chances despite the pawn deficit. By retreating the king, Black preserves that advantage and keeps the evaluation level as White prepares to regroup; White's Ng5 on the next move will soon probe whether Black can maintain the edge in practice.

per_ply.system_comment: 14.Ng5 is the most accurate move, holding the balance (+0.00, Stockfish:16) along [pv:Ng5 Nxc4 Qh5 Kg7], at the cost of a continuation that may leave White with a hanging piece. A comparable option was 14.Qc1, which leads to equality after [pv:Qc1 Ng8 Nh5 Nxc4 Qf4+], though Ng5 remains White's strongest choice on the most testing line.

Bxg8 is the most accurate move, holding the balance (+0.12, Stockfish:16) along [pv:Bxg8 Rxh7 Nxh7 Qxg8 Ng5], though deeper in that line Black's king may become safer. That beats 16.e5, which leads to a clear advantage for Black after [pv:e5 Nxc4 Qh5 Nxf6 exf6+], where White would immediately establish a strong knight on f6 but could later end up with a rook and pawn for two bishops.

per_ply.human_comment: Urusov is now facing a difficult choice.
per_ply.system_comment: 17.Nxh7 is the most accurate move, holding the balance (+0.18, Stockfish:16) after [pv:Nxh7 Qxg8 Ng5 Nc6 d5], as Ng5 in the line may set White up to target the knight on c6. Bxh7 was a comparable option that leads to equality via [pv:Bxh7 Qxf6 Rc1 Qh4 Bf5], where White immediately has a rook and two pawns for a bishop and knight and could later target the bishop on c8, but Nxh7 keeps sharper chances without settling for that structural trade.

Black missed the chance to capture on g8 and make the king safe—worth doing while White's monarch is still under pressure. With 17...Qh4 instead, Black keeps White's king under pressure and leaves a piece hanging, but now White is up the exchange, and this move concedes a clear advantage to White: (+0.18 → +0.76, Stockfish:16) along [pv:Qh4 Qf3 Kxg8 Nf6+ Kg7]. 17...Qxg8 leads to equality after [pv:Qxg8 Ng5 Nc6 d5 Ne5].

The most accurate move, 18.Qf3, maintains White's advantage (+0.77, Stockfish:16) along [pv:Qf3 Kxg8 Nf6+ Kg7 Nd5], with White holding a rook and two pawns for two bishops — an imbalance that often favors the side with the rook in simplified endings. e5 is a comparable option that leads to a slight advantage for White via [pv:e5 Bg4 Qd3 Rxg8 Nf6], where White is up the exchange and may set up targeting the rook on g8, but Qf3 keeps the clearer edge.

Black's most accurate move is 18...Kxg8, though it still leads to a clear advantage for White (+0.76, Stockfish:16) after [pv:Kxg8 Nf6+ Kg7 Nd5 Nc6], where the follow-up checks and Nd5 keep White firmly in control. That holds up clearly better than 18...Be6, which would give White a winning advantage along [pv:Be6 Bxe6 Qxh7 Rac1 Nc6].

The most accurate move, Nf6+, maintains White's advantage (+0.73, Stockfish:16) along [pv:Nf6+ Kg7 Nd5 Nc6 Nxb6], steering toward a line that may deny Black the bishop-pair edge—two bishops usually coordinate more strongly on open lines—in return for the risk that Black's pieces could become more actively placed deeper in the variation. Qf8+ is clearly weaker, leading only to equality with [pv:Qf8+ Kxh7 Qf7+ Kh6 Qf8+], immediately targeting the bishop on c8 yet unable to preserve White's edge the way Nf6+ does.

Nf4+ is the strongest move, maintaining White's advantage (+0.73, Stockfish:16) along [pv:Nf4+ Kg7 Nd5 Nc6 Nxb6]. The check may set up targeting the knight on c6 deeper in the line, though in return Black's king is safer for now. Ng3 leads to equality after [pv:Ng3 Nc6 d5 Ne5 Qf8], where White could only threaten the bishop on c8 further down the variation—a weaker plan than keeping the sharper initiative that pays off when Black later plays...Be6.

This move makes matters worse, and White now has a winning advantage (+1.08 → +2.39, Stockfish:16). Nxb6 punishes it, and after [pv:Be6 Nxb6 axb6 d5 Bg4] the line may leave White with a rook and two pawns for two pieces. Black missed the chance to keep pieces actively placed with Kg8, which leads to a clear advantage for White [pv:Kg8 Qc3 Bd7 Rae1 Nc6].

Nxb6 is the strongest continuation, maintaining White's advantage (+2.45, Stockfish:16) as the follow-up [pv:Nxb6 axb6 d5 Qg4 dxe6] may leave the king safer and could produce a passed pawn on f3—passed pawns often decide late endings. In return, Black immediately establishes a strong knight on a5 and activates both rooks on the open files. Rac1 also leads to a clear advantage for White but is clearly weaker: [pv:Rac1 Bxd5 exd5 Kg7 Rc3] activates the rooks at once yet may only settle into a rook and two pawns for a bishop and knight, without the same drive toward king safety and the passed pawn.

23...axb6 gives White a winning advantage (+2.29, Stockfish:16), and after [pv:axb6 d5 Bg4 Qf7+ Kh8] Black achieves little while the line may leave his back rank vulnerable—a serious problem when the king lacks escape squares. White can answer with 24.d5 and keep pressing. The comparable 23...cxb6 also gives White a winning advantage; it would have established a strong knight on a5 immediately, though White's pieces could become more passive in the continuation [pv:cxb6 d5 Qg4 dxe6 Qxf3].

The best move, 24.d5, maintains White's advantage (+2.21, Stockfish:16) and pushes the fight after [pv:d5 Qg4 dxe6 Qxf3 gxf3]: Black now has a hanging piece—a target that's costly to cover—and his pieces are passive. In return, the line may leave White with a hanging piece and doubled e-pawns. Rac1 is a comparable option that gives White a winning advantage [pv:Rac1 Nc6 d5 Ne5 Rxc7+], putting the rooks on the open files and potentially yielding a rook and three pawns for two pieces.

24...Bg8 gives White a winning advantage (+2.14, Stockfish:16), and the bishop retreat does little for Black: after [pv:Bg8 Qc3 c5 f4 b5] he may lose his strong knight while White's passed pawn could push dangerously forward—a far-advanced passer can tie down pieces and decide endings. Qg4 is a comparable option that also gives White a winning advantage, immediately leaving a piece hanging and targeting the queen on f3 via [pv:Qg4 dxe6 Qxf3 gxf3 Re8].

25...Qe7 makes matters worse for Black, and White now has a decisive advantage (+1.97 → +3.49, Stockfish:16), with play likely continuing [pv:Qe7 Qh3+ Kg7 Rc3 Bh7]. Black missed the potential to leave White with a hanging piece and to target the rook on c3 with c6, which gives White a winning advantage, along [pv:c6 Rc3 Kh8 Qd1 Qf6].

Rfe1 gives White a winning advantage as a comparable option that could leave Black's king under pressure and set up targeting of the bishop on g6 in [pv:Rfe1 Bf7 Re3 Bg6 Qg4].
